blocks.x: Serrated bread knives may seem like specialized kitchen tools, but you’d be hard-pressed to slice that beautiful loaf of sourdough you brought home without one. Unlike standard kitchen knives, serrated knives have, well, serrations—a line of individually sharpened teeth along the edges that dig into whatever you’re cutting with each stroke. This sawing action easily cuts through a soft bread crumb without smooshing it, and it’s also helpful for slicing delicate tomato skin or peeling a watermelon.

For years, the common thought was that a good serrated knife didn’t have to be expensive, and we generally agree—you can find an affordable bread knife that’ll do the job well and free up more of your knife budget to invest in the rest of your knife set. Some of that is because part of what makes a chef’s knife expensive, the high quality steel forged to hold a fine, sharp edge for a long time, isn’t as much of a thing for serrated knives. The design of the teeth makes it so that the blade can still function even if it isn’t that sharp; that’s not really the case for straight edge knives. And, because sharpening a serrated knife is a much more involved process than sharpening a straight edge knife, some people think it’s better to replace a serrated knife after several years rather than try to maintain it.

After testing 36 bread knives over the past few years, I think it’s worth investing in a high-end bread knife that’ll stay sharper longer, with blade geometry that makes slicing as easy as possible. And so I recommend one of those along with a variety of more affordable picks below. Regardless, the best bread knives at any price point are sharp, long enough for large loaves of bread, and sturdy in the hand. The top picks below all aced that criteria even with long-term testing.

New in this update: We replaced the top pick in this piece after long-term testing of our favorite knives, and because of pricing and availability issues with a longtime favorite brand Tojiro. We also updated additional reviews, including on knives from Made In, Winco, and Mac after more testing. Finally we added a section on serrated knife sharpening and tested a well-liked serrated knife sharpening rod.
Best bread knife overall: Mac Superior Series 10.5" bread knife

blocks.c: Image may contain: Blade, Weapon, Knife, Dagger, and Cutlery

blocks.x: Long blade makes slicing through wide bread loaves easy
On the pricier end of the spectrum

Knife length: 15.38"
Blade length: 10.75"
Weight: 6.6 oz.

What we love: Mac’s Superior Series bread knife features an extra-long curved blade that makes slicing bread a breeze. Even the crustiest, oversized miche loaves were no match for this knife. It features rounded teeth that cut easily into the crust without snagging, making each stroke smoother and more deliberate. It also sliced neatly through tomato skin and glide effortlessly through the pulp, delivering perfectly uniform tomato slices.

The Mac is made from high-carbon stainless steel that will keep an edge longer—a plus because serrated knives are so labor-intensive to sharpen. The curve to the blade is another excellent design choice. That curve adds cutting force to the knife because the belly extends about half an inch beyond the handle, creating immediate leverage with each stroke. In long-term testing, I found that Mac’s Superior Series offered sustained performance that cheaper knives just couldn’t match, bumping this knife into our top-pick slot.

What we’d leave: My biggest gripe about this knife is the price point and handle construction. While the blocky handle scales are comfortable, it seems reasonable to expect a $100 knife to have an integrated bolster and nicer finish. For those looking for a nicer handle and are willing to spend money, you can check out the Mac Professional Series below.

NOTE: The Mac Superior series is sometimes listed as the Mac Professional series on Amazon and other large marketplaces. It is not! The Professional series has a metal bolster between the blade and the handle. No bolster, not Professional. The actual Professional series knife should also cost about 50% more than the Superior series model.
The best cheap (but very good) bread knife: Mercer Culinary M23210 10" Bread Knife

blocks.c: Mercer Culinary M23210 Millennia Black Handle, 10-Inch Wide Wavy Edge, Bread Knife

blocks.x:
Knife length: 15.5"
Blade length: 10"
Weight: 5.9 oz.

What we love: Premium bread knives have their perks, but a good one doesn’t have to break the bank. The Mercer Culinary Millennia 10" bread knife is less than $20, and it’s the one we use most frequently in the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen. “This bread knife came in the kit bag I got in culinary school, and I am still using it today,” food director Chris Morocco says. “It won’t split atoms, but it is dependable, and for this price, you will love it all the more.” It has deep, wide serrations, also known as a wavy edge, as opposed to the pointy teeth you see on the Wüsthof or Tojiro.

Instead of a wooden handle, the ergonomic handle of the Mercer is made from a combination of rubber and plastic. While this knife isn’t full-tang (no knife at this price is), it still feels stable and comfortable to hold. Our editors have used this knife for every slicing task you can imagine: crusty bread, pineapple, ripe tomatoes, overstuffed BLTs—and it always gets the job done.

What we’d leave: This knife performed admirably for its price point, but it was the least sharp of our other two winning bread knives, requiring a bit more effort to cut crustier loaves. Some people also didn’t like the Mercer’s plastic handle, which wasn’t as comfortable as our other picks.

A worthy splurge: Shun Classic 9" Bread Knife
High carbon steel will stay sharper longer

Knife length: 14"
Blade length: 9"
Weight: 6.8 oz.

What we love: While chef’s knives are often praised for their steel quality and appearance, bread knives are typically prized for their functionality. While you don’t need to spend as much on a bread knife to get top-tier performance, we really loved the total package from Shun’s Classic line bread knife. It’s made from Damascus steel with a VG-MAX core, which is a much higher-carbon-content steel than most bread knives. This means that the serrated edge of the knife is less likely to dull over time—key for a knife that needs to be maintained professionally to keep sharp edges. In testing, it sliced tomatoes beautifully thin, and even the crustiest sourdough provided almost zero resistance.

We also appreciated the height of the blade, which provided some extra heft and cutting force without adding extra weight. Finally, the Japanese wa-style handle was comfortable to grip when you needed a little extra leverage. Because there’s no palm swell or shape to the handle, it lets the user find the position that’s most comfortable for them. Shun’s bread knife might be pricier than our other top picks, but the price definitely matches the performance and knife quality. If you’re looking for a serrated knife that will stay sharper for longer, then this might be the right pick for you.

What we’d leave: The 9" blade was plenty long for most loaves of bread, but wider boules were tricky to cut all the way across without having to angle the knife. It’s hard to ignore how expensive this knife is. While it does have the highest quality fit and finish of our winners, its performance boost over our two budget picks might not quite be enough for some people. Still, if you’re picky about the details of knife construction and steel quality, this knife justifies its price point.
